title: The mountain of light (Matthew 17:1–8)
hookLine: on a mountain his face shines like the sun, and Peter wants to build tents
carry: you can't stay on the mountain

cards: A sunrise that stops the car. A newborn's first cry. The last chord of a song, before anyone claps.
Some moments seem lit from the inside, and nobody wants them to end. Jesus takes just three of his friends, Peter, James and John, up a high mountain, away from everyone.
Matthew doesn't name it; tradition says it was Mount Tabor, in Galilee, a round hill rising alone from the plain. And up there, in front of them, something happens.

teach.b: He was transfigured before them, Matthew says, in the King James Bible: "and his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light."
The Greek word is metamorphoo, the root of our metamorphosis: changed in form. The Latin became transfiguration.
Two more figures appear, talking with him: Moses, who gave the law, and Elijah, the great prophet. Some readers see the law and the prophets standing together on one mountain.

Then Peter, who never seems to stay quiet for long, gets practical: "Lord, it is good for us to be here: if thou wilt, let us make here three tabernacles; one for thee, and one for Moses, and one for Elias."
Tabernacles means tents, shelters. Let's build. Let's stay.
While he's still talking, a bright cloud covers them, and a voice says what it said at the river: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear ye him." Hear him, not build for him.
The disciples fall on their faces, terrified. Then the gentlest moment. Jesus comes and touches them: "Arise, and be not afraid."
They look up, and there's no one but Jesus.
They walk back down, and waiting at the bottom is a crowd, and a father with a sick boy.

teach.h: HIS FACE DID SHINE AS THE SUN.
teach.b: The light doesn't last. Life resumes. Orthodox Christians give this story a special place, and speak of the light on the mountain as God's own light, which the saints can come to share.
Many churches keep the feast on August sixth.

how: Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches keep the feast of the Transfiguration on August 6, and many Protestant churches read the story on the Sunday before Lent. On that day many Orthodox churches bless the first fruits of the harvest, often grapes.

games.q: you're Peter. your teacher's face is shining like the sun, and Moses and Elijah are standing there talking with him. what do you say?
o: it's good to be here. let's build three tents.
we should go and get the others.
games.why: Peter offers to build three tabernacles, and while he's still speaking, a bright cloud covers them and a voice says: hear ye him.

practice: Close your eyes if you like, and bring back one moment of pure light in your own life, religious or not: a morning, a face, a song, a place, a silence, the light, the sound, the air.
Stay with it for a few breaths, then gently let it go, and notice you're still carrying something of it. If you pray, you can give thanks for it.

wordCard.voice: Transfiguration. From the Latin, and behind it the Greek for metamorphosis: changed in form. On a mountain his face shone like the sun.

orig.note: Greek: he was transfigured, changed in form. The root of our word metamorphosis.
